Title: Qwen3 8B
Summary: Official Q4/Q5/Q8 download sizes, native and extended context, and practical memory planning for Qwen3 8B.
Body Markdown:
## Which checkpoint should I download?

Use **Qwen/Qwen3-8B** and the publisher’s GGUF files. This checkpoint supports thinking and non-thinking modes. Keep that mode fixed when comparing results; thinking output uses tokens and time before the final answer.

## Can I use its full context window?

Qwen lists 32,768 native tokens and up to 131,072 with YaRN. Extended context needs explicit runtime support and more memory. The Finder’s 64K planning limit does not verify YaRN support. See [[guides/context-length|context length]].

## What if it loads but runs out of memory?

Close other GPU workloads and reduce context. If needed, use a smaller file or partial CPU offload. For Macs or CPU-only setups, select the appropriate mode in the Finder; installed RAM is not dedicated VRAM.

Title: gpt-oss-20b
Summary: Understand total versus active parameters, MXFP4 checkpoint size, Harmony support and local memory requirements.
Body Markdown:
## Which format and runtime do I need?

Use a runtime with explicit **gpt-oss, MXFP4 and Harmony** support. MXFP4 is not interchangeable with an ordinary GGUF Q4_K_M conversion. Harmony must handle reasoning and final-answer channels; a generic chat template can give misleading output.

## How should I choose context and reasoning effort?

The publisher lists up to 131,072 context tokens. Runtime support and memory are separate limits. Start with the context you need, and keep low, medium or high reasoning effort fixed when comparing time to an answer.

## Does the active parameter count reduce the memory needed?

The model has about 20.9B total parameters and 3.6B active per token. The active count describes computation, not the amount of weights that must be stored. It does not establish inference speed.

Title: Q4 vs Q5
Summary: Choose between Q4_K_M and Q5_K_M using real file sizes, memory headroom, context needs and a practical quality comparison.
Body Markdown:
## What Q4 and Q5 mean

Quantization stores model weights with reduced precision to lower their memory and download requirements. In common GGUF filenames, Q4_K_M and Q5_K_M describe different quantization recipes used by llama.cpp.

Q4_K_M is usually the smaller choice for the same checkpoint and conversion family. Q5_K_M generally stores more precision and needs more space. The labels do not mean every value is stored in exactly four or five bits: scales, metadata and tensors treated at other precisions also contribute.

The [llama.cpp quantization implementation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/llama-quant.cpp) defines these recipes. Different formats with a “4-bit” label, such as the MXFP4 expert weights in [[models/gpt-oss-20b|gpt-oss-20b]], should not be treated as interchangeable.

## A real download-size comparison

Qwen's [official Qwen3 8B GGUF file list](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF/tree/main) shows:

- Q4_K_M: about 5.03 GB.
- Q5_K_M: about 5.85 GB.
- Difference: about 0.82 GB, or 16% more weights than Q4_K_M.

These rounded decimal sizes are specific to that model and conversion. Q5 is not universally 16% or 25% larger. Compare the actual files for the checkpoint you want.

For the larger [[models/qwen2-5-coder-14b|Qwen2.5-Coder 14B]], the extra weight memory is more consequential on a tight GPU budget. The trade-off should be assessed alongside context, rather than choosing a quant by name alone.

## File size is not total runtime memory

Loading a quantized model also needs working buffers and the context/KV cache. Some runtimes reserve capacity for the configured context when loading; others grow allocations as they process tokens.

Reducing the precision of the model weights does not automatically change the precision of the KV cache. These are separate settings in runtimes such as [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md).

If Q5 fits at 4K but fails at 16K, the longer context may account for the difference. The download has not changed. See [[guides/context-length|why context length affects memory]].

## When to start with Q4_K_M

Q4_K_M is a sensible initial test when memory is constrained, when you need to retain a useful context, or when Q5 would require additional CPU offload.

For example, an [[hardware/rtx-3060-12gb|RTX 3060 12 GB]] running a larger model has less room for extra precision than the same card running [[models/qwen3-8b|Qwen3 8B]]. Check the runtime's actual allocation instead of assuming all installed VRAM is available.

A smaller quant that stays within the intended device budget may be more convenient than a larger one that changes the offload arrangement. This is a testable setup choice, not a universal speed ranking.

## When Q5_K_M is worth testing

Try Q5_K_M when you have enough space for weights, context and buffers, and you want to compare whether it helps your workload. More stored precision can reduce quantization error, but it does not guarantee that every answer improves.

Use the same model version, chat template and generation settings. For coding, compare correctness with tests. For extraction, compare against known answers. For writing, judge the result against the constraints you actually care about.

Avoid comparing one Q4 model with a different Q5 model and attributing the whole difference to quantization.

## A practical comparison

Begin with Q4_K_M and a representative context length. Record memory use, time to the first useful response and the outcome on several prompts. Repeat with Q5_K_M while keeping the other settings fixed.

If the Q5 setup changes CPU offload, record that too; it is part of the result. Keep the quant that delivers useful output within your memory and latency needs.

[Compare memory estimates in the Finder](https://localllmfinder.com/). The final decision should use the exact artifact and runtime, rather than a generic claim that one quant is always best.

Title: Context length
Summary: Why longer context increases runtime memory, how KV caches differ from weights, and how to check a useful local context limit.
Body Markdown:
## What context length includes

A model's context window is the token budget available for the conversation it processes. It includes instructions, chat history, pasted documents, tool results and generated output. Reasoning output can consume that budget too.

Tokens are pieces of encoded text, not a fixed number of words. Leave room for the reply instead of filling the entire window with input. A conversation that approaches the limit may be truncated, rejected or handled with a runtime-specific shifting mechanism.

## Three limits to check

There are three separate questions:

- What context does the model publisher document?
- What context does the downloaded artifact and runtime support and configure?
- What context can your hardware hold at the selected quant and workload?

For example, [[models/qwen3-8b|Qwen3 8B]] documents 32,768 tokens natively and an extended 131,072 with YaRN. A higher slider value does not itself implement that scaling.

[[models/gpt-oss-20b|gpt-oss-20b]] also has a published long-context ceiling, but the local memory budget and runtime configuration still need to be checked. Local LLM Finder's catalogue limit is an estimate input, not proof that a particular app implements the full model limit.

## Why the same file needs more memory

During autoregressive generation, attention uses a key/value cache so the model can reuse information from earlier tokens. The [Hugging Face cache documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/kv_cache) describes cache strategies and their memory trade-offs.

For ordinary full-attention layers, a useful first approximation is that KV-cache storage increases with the number of cached tokens, layer count, key/value heads, head size and bytes per cache value. Grouped-query attention changes the head count that matters.

Models with sliding-window attention, compressed caches or other architectures can behave differently. Batching and simultaneous conversations also change the memory budget. A simple per-token estimate is therefore guidance, not a universal allocation formula.

The weights file stays the same size when you raise context. The cache and other runtime allocations are what change.

## An illustrative memory budget

Consider a hypothetical setup with 5 GB of weights, 0.5 GB of other allocations and a full-attention cache that uses 0.75 GB at 4K tokens:

- At 4K, the example totals 6.25 GB.
- At 16K, four times as many cached tokens would use about 3 GB of cache.
- The example then totals 8.5 GB, while the weights remain 5 GB.

These numbers explain the relationship; they are not measurements of Qwen3, gpt-oss or an RTX 3060. Real runtimes can allocate buffers differently or reserve the configured cache up front.

## Weight quantization and cache quantization are separate

Choosing Q4_K_M instead of Q5_K_M primarily changes stored weights. It does not automatically lower the KV-cache precision. [llama.cpp's server documentation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md) exposes context and key/value cache controls separately.

Cache quantization or offload can reduce device-memory pressure in supported configurations, but may affect performance or output. Verify support for your model and backend before changing those controls.

[[guides/q4-vs-q5|Q4 vs Q5]] covers the weight trade-off. Keeping a useful context can matter more to your task than spending the last available memory on a larger quant.

## Set a useful context and verify it

For an initial local test, 4K is a manageable starting point when your task fits. Increase it for longer conversations or documents after checking memory, the model limit and the runtime's configuration.

In Ollama, the [context-length documentation](https://docs.ollama.com/context-length) explains configuration and checking the allocated context with `ollama ps`. Other runtimes have their own logs and controls. Defaults can change, so check the allocation rather than assuming it matches the publisher's maximum.

- Choose a representative prompt and reserve reply space.
- Record quant, context and CPU/GPU offload.
- Test a longer prompt, not only an empty conversation.
- Reduce context or shorten the retained history if you exceed memory.
- Compare time to a useful answer as well as whether the model loads.

On an [[hardware/rtx-3060-12gb|RTX 3060 12 GB]], this check can make the difference between a practical configuration and an allocation failure. [Use the Finder to compare context estimates](https://localllmfinder.com/), then confirm them in your runtime.
